newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Saudi Arabia pledge to develop ties.
newsitem.headline: France, Saudi Arabia pledge to develop ties.

text.p: France and Saudi Arabia pledged on Thursday to develop a new partnership including political, economic and defence cooperation.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said after talks with visiting Saudi Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan that both men had seen eye to eye on many Middle East issues.

"On the peace process as on the attitude towards Iraq or Iran, France has positions which are very clear and often very close to Saudi Arabia," Juppe told reporters after meeting Sultan, who was on the second day of a three-day visit.

A communiqu released after Sultan met President Jacques Chirac said the two men pledged "to develop and reinforce relations in all domains, notably in the framework of a real partnership, their political and economic...and security cooperation".

The statement made no specific mention of arms sales but Paris is trying to convince Saudi Arabia to buy Leclerc main battle tanks made by Giat Industries, similar to those sold for $3.62 billion to the neighbouring United Arab Emirates in 1993.
Paris is vying with Britain and the United States for the huge arms contract. Its tanks were tested in the kingdom's desert this summer at Saudi Arabia's request.
Diplomats said France also hoped to turn a memorandum of understanding on radar and surveillance systems for zone and border defence into contracts.
"We have made much progress on many economic issues. All the dossiers are moving forward and everything has been examined in detail by ministers," Juppe said.
The joint statement said the two sides favoured moves towards a global, just and lasting peace in the Middle East.

Alluding to tension over Israeli plans for new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem, the statement called for the status quo not to be disturbed in the Holy City and called for respect of Palestinian rights.
The two also called for the respect of Iraqi territorial sovereignty in the framework of U.N. sanctions against that country and condemned terrorism.

On Wednesday, French Defence Minister Charles Millon said after meeting Sultan: "We will enter into the subject of a partnership between Saudi Arabia and France in the defence field and other domains."

"There will be repercussions in the fields of investment, judicial procedures and equipment but those are not the main reasons for the visit. First and foremost, we have political objectives," Millon said.

Sultan said after meeting Millon that his country had embarked on a "policy of economic restabilisation" with the United States and Britain which would also be applied to France, probably with better formulas.

"We will see the birth of joint industries with French and Saudi capital. Capital and investments consolidate friendship between peoples. We hope to succeed in cooperation with France in all domains," he said.

France, which buys a quarter of its oil from Saudi Arabia, is the kingdom's third biggest arms supplier after the United States and Britain. Weapons sales average $1.2 billion a year, roughly equivalent to its civilian exports.

Chirac met Saudi King Fahd in Riyadh in July and both said their talks had ensured continued cooperation at all levels. France took part in a U.S.-led Western military alliance that drove Iraqi troops out of Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.
